name: HC-05 Bluetooth Serial Module
desc: Gives an Arduino a wireless serial link to an Android phone or a PC. Classic Bluetooth only.
note: Does NOT work with iPhones: iOS apps can't use classic Bluetooth serial. For iPhone, use an ESP32's Bluetooth LE or Wi-Fi.

warn.5: HC-05 RX is 3.3V. Put a voltage divider (1kΩ + 2kΩ) between the Arduino's TX and the HC-05's RX.

name: nRF24L01+ 2.4GHz Radio
desc: Cheap radio modules that let two boards talk wirelessly (up to ~100 m in the open). Great for remote controls.
note: Solder a 10µF capacitor across VCC and GND right on the module, or it drops out randomly.

warn.5: nRF24L01 must be powered from 3.3V. 5V destroys it. Its data pins are fine with 5V signals.

name: IR Receiver (VS1838B) + Remote
desc: A small infrared receiver plus a credit-card remote. Control your project from the couch, or read your TV remote's buttons.
note: Bare receivers differ in pin order. Check the datasheet or module labels (OUT, GND, VCC).

name: RC522 RFID Reader + Card & Tag
desc: Reads the ID of tap cards and key tags (13.56MHz). Make a card-activated door, attendance logger or magic-wand game.
note: Usually needs header pins soldered on.

warn.5: RC522 must be powered from 3.3V. Its pins are 3.3V. Many tutorials wire an Uno directly, but a level shifter is the safe choice.

name: 433MHz RF Transmitter + Receiver Pair
desc: A very cheap one-way radio link for sending simple codes between boards, like a wireless doorbell.
note: Range improves a lot with a 17 cm wire antenna soldered to each module.

warn.3.3: The 433MHz receiver runs on 5V and outputs 5V. Use a voltage divider (1kΩ + 2kΩ) into a 3.3V board.

name: microSD Card Module (SPI)
desc: Lets your board save data to a microSD card, like sensor logs your PC can open in Excel.
note: Power this common blue module from 5V, even with ESP32/Pico. Format the card as FAT32.

name: DS3231 Real-Time Clock (ZS-042)
desc: A very accurate clock with a coin battery, so your project knows the date and time even after power-off.
note: This board tries to charge its coin cell. With a regular CR2032 (not rechargeable), remove the charging diode or resistor, or use an LIR2032.

name: HC-06 Bluetooth Serial Module (slave)
desc: A simpler version of the HC-05 that can only accept connections. Android/PC only.
note: Doesn't work with iPhones (classic Bluetooth serial).

warn.5: HC-06 RX is 3.3V. Put a voltage divider (1kΩ + 2kΩ) between the board's TX and the HC-06 RX.

name: HM-10 Bluetooth LE Module
desc: A Bluetooth Low Energy serial module that DOES work with iPhones (using a BLE terminal app).
note: Many cheap "HM-10" boards are clones (CC41-A) with different commands. Look for the CC2541 chip.

warn.5: HM-10 RX is 3.3V. Put a voltage divider (1kΩ + 2kΩ) on its RX from a 5V board.

name: ESP-01 Wi-Fi Module (ESP8266)
desc: A tiny ESP8266 Wi-Fi module that can add Wi-Fi to an Arduino or run code by itself.
note: Programming needs a USB adapter. An Uno's 3.3V pin is too weak to power it: use a 3.3V regulator module.

warn.5: ESP-01 is 3.3V only: 5V on VCC or its pins can destroy it. Use a 3.3V regulator and a divider on its RX.

name: LoRa Module SX1278 (Ra-02, 433MHz)
desc: Long-range radio: small messages over kilometres in open areas. Great for remote sensors.
note: Always connect the antenna before powering it. Check local radio rules for your frequency.

warn.5: The SX1278 is 3.3V only, including its pins. Use a 3.3V board (ESP32/Pico) or a level shifter.

name: nRF24L01+ PA/LNA (long range, antenna)
desc: The nRF24 with an amplifier and antenna: up to ~1 km in open air.
note: Draws more current than the basic module: use the nRF24 adapter board or a 3.3V regulator, plus a 10µF capacitor.

warn.5: Power it from 3.3V only (5V destroys it). The adapter board makes this easy.

name: nRF24L01 Adapter Board (5V → 3.3V)
desc: A socket board with its own 3.3V regulator and capacitors: power your nRF24 from 5V safely and stably.

name: RDM6300 125kHz RFID Reader
desc: Reads the older 125kHz key fobs and cards (EM4100) and sends their ID over serial.

warn.3.3: The RDM6300 runs on 5V and its TX outputs 5V. Use a voltage divider (1kΩ + 2kΩ) into a 3.3V board.

name: PN532 NFC/RFID Module (V3)
desc: Reads and writes NFC tags and cards (13.56MHz). Supports I2C, SPI or UART via small switches.

name: MCP2515 CAN Bus Module
desc: Talk to CAN bus networks, the system cars and machines use.
note: Don't connect to a real car's CAN bus unless you know exactly what you're doing.

warn.3.3: This module's transceiver needs 5V. With 3.3V boards, use a level shifter on SPI or a 3.3V CAN module.

name: MAX485 RS-485 Module
desc: Sends serial data over long twisted-pair wires (hundreds of metres), as factories do.

warn.3.3: MAX485 runs on 5V and outputs 5V on RO. Use a divider into a 3.3V board, or a 3.3V transceiver (MAX3485).

name: W5500 Ethernet Module
desc: Wired internet (RJ45) for your board: more reliable than Wi-Fi for always-on gadgets.

warn.5: W5500 logic is 3.3V (its pins are 5V-tolerant on most modules). Power it from 3.3V unless your board has a regulator.

name: USB-to-TTL Serial Adapter (CH340)
desc: Connects boards without USB (Pro Mini, ESP-01) to your PC for uploading and Serial Monitor.
note: Set the jumper to match your board (3.3V or 5V) before connecting.

name: ESP32-CAM-MB Programmer Board
desc: A small USB board the ESP32-CAM plugs into, for uploading code and power.

name: DS1307 Real-Time Clock (Tiny RTC)
desc: A cheaper real-time clock with a coin cell. Less accurate than the DS3231 (it can drift seconds per day).

warn.3.3: DS1307 boards need 5V and pull I2C up to 5V. Use a level shifter with 3.3V boards (or choose a DS3231).

name: TCA9548A I2C Multiplexer (8 channels)
desc: Lets you connect several sensors that share the same I2C address, like two OLEDs.

name: AT24C256 EEPROM Module (32KB)
desc: Small memory chip that keeps data without power: save settings, scores and logs.

name: RXB6 433MHz Superheterodyne Receiver
desc: A much more sensitive 433MHz receiver than the basic one: longer range for doorbells and remotes.
note: Power it from the same voltage as your board, so its output matches your board's logic level.
